sceneHappening: A first warning: do not drift from so great a salvation; Jesus shared our flesh to free us and to help
summary: "Therefore we ought to pay greater attention to the things that were heard, lest perhaps we drift away. For if the word spoken through angels proved steadfast, and every transgression and disobedience received a just penalty, how will we escape if we neglect so great a salvation—which at the first having been spoken through the Lord, was confirmed to us by those who heard, God also testifying with them, both by signs and wonders, by various works of power and by gifts of the Holy Spirit?" God did not subject "the world to come" to angels, but quoting Psalm 8, "What is man, that you think of him?... You made him a little lower than the angels... You have put all things in subjection under his feet." "But now we don't see all things subjected to him, yet. But we see him who has been made a little lower than the angels, Jesus, because of the suffering of death crowned with glory and honor, that by the grace of God he should taste of death for everyone." It was fitting "in bringing many children to glory, to make the author of their salvation perfect through sufferings." He calls them brothers, "since then the children have shared in flesh and blood, he also himself in the same way partook of the same, that through death he might bring to nothing him who had the power of death, that is, the devil, and might deliver all of them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage." "Therefore he was obligated in all things to be made like his brothers, that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest in things pertaining to God, to make atonement for the sins of the people. For in that he himself has suffered being tempted, he is able to help those who are tempted."
whySettingMatters: This is the first of five warnings in the letter. The picture "drift away" (2:1) is of a boat slipping past its mooring, not a sudden storm; the danger is slow neglect. Verses 5-9 read Psalm 8 as speaking first of humanity and then of Jesus, the one human who is already "crowned with glory and honor," and whose present rule is not yet visible ("we don't see all things subjected to him, yet"). The word translated "author" (archegos) means a pioneer or leader who goes first and opens the way (also 12:2; Acts 3:15; 5:31); "made perfect" (teleioo) does not mean he had a flaw but that he was brought to the full goal through suffering, a theme that returns often in the letter. The chapter introduces the idea of Jesus as "high priest" for the first time (2:17), a topic that will take up the middle of the book. The "fear of death" that enslaves people (2:15) and the devil's hold on death are placed in the background of the Jewish and Greek worlds the readers lived in. Verse 16 speaks of Jesus helping "the offspring of Abraham" and not angels; this is consistent with a Jewish-Christian audience, though "offspring of Abraham" is read in Galatians 3:29 as all who belong to Christ.

people.note: Warns the readers, counting himself with them ("we").
Made a little lower than the angels, tasted death for everyone, and is a merciful and faithful high priest.
In danger of drifting from so great a salvation.
His offspring are the ones Jesus helps.

questions: "Lest we drift away": most drifting is slow and unnoticed. What small neglect tends to lead you away?
Psalm 8 asks what humans are that God cares for them. How does the author use it to describe Jesus?
"He is not ashamed to call them brothers." What does it mean to you that Jesus claims kinship?
Jesus was "made perfect through sufferings" and "is able to help those who are tempted." How does his suffering equip him to help?
